title: Recommendation System
summary: Select and rank relevant items while balancing immediate engagement, discovery, and system constraints.
prompt: Design a recommendation system that produces a personalized set of items for a consumer home surface.
productGoal: Help users discover useful items with less search effort.
Define the surface, session context, and acceptable recommendation latency.
Include diversity, safety, and creator or catalog health as product constraints.
predictionTarget: Predict a useful interaction such as qualified engagement, not just an easy-to-measure impression click.
Use a multi-stage objective if immediate and longer-term outcomes differ.
Define eligibility before ranking so the model never scores forbidden items.
successMetrics: Offline: ranking metrics such as NDCG, MAP, recall at candidate cutoff, and segment coverage.
Online: qualified engagement or downstream conversion appropriate to the product.
Guardrails: hides, complaints, latency, concentration, and exposure diversity.
dataSources: Impressions, interactions, item metadata, user context, and inventory state.
Point-in-time joins so training only sees information available at recommendation time.
Explicitly distinguish missing events from negative preference.
labeling: Define a time window after an impression for outcomes to mature.
Correct for position and exposure bias where feasible.
Sample negatives from eligible shown or retrievable items with known context.
features: User history summaries, item attributes, freshness, context, and interaction crosses.
Embeddings can represent users and items but need version and freshness ownership.
Avoid sensitive attributes unless there is a justified, reviewed use.
baseline: Start with popular eligible items segmented by context or recency.
A simple collaborative or content-based model provides a meaningful second baseline.
modelDiscussion: A two-tower model is one candidate-generation option when the catalog is large.
A richer ranker can combine user, item, and context features on a smaller candidate set.
Post-ranking policy can enforce diversity, availability, and safety constraints.
training: Build versioned examples with point-in-time features and reproducible splits.
Retrain on a cadence linked to behavior and catalog change.
Track data, feature, code, and model versions for rollback.
evaluation: Measure candidate recall separately from ranker quality.
Report cold-user, cold-item, and major segment results.
Use online experiments to validate product impact rather than assuming offline gains transfer.
serving: Retrieve candidates from an embedding or heuristic index, then rank and post-process.
Cache safe components such as item representations, not entire personalized responses without clear keys.
Define fallbacks for feature-store, retrieval, and model timeouts.
monitoring: Monitor feature freshness, candidate counts, score distributions, latency, and fallback rate.
Join delayed outcomes to predictions for quality by segment.
Watch catalog and exposure concentration, not only average engagement.
feedbackLoop: Log impressions and positions so absence of interaction is interpretable.
Use exploration carefully to learn about underexposed items.
Prevent repeated recommendations from creating self-reinforcing popularity loops.
failureModes: Candidate generation misses the best items.
Training labels overvalue clickbait or high positions.
Fresh inventory is absent from the index.
A feature outage silently sends default values to the ranker.
tradeoffs: Freshness competes with precomputation and cacheability.
Model complexity competes with latency and debuggability.
Personalization depth competes with privacy and cold-start robustness.
extensions: How would session-based intent change the design?
How would you introduce exploration?
How would multi-objective ranking be governed?
interviewChecklist: Framed the product decision and baseline.
Included quality, guardrail, and feedback-loop monitoring.

title: Search Ranking System
summary: Rank retrieved results for a query while preserving relevance, latency, and marketplace or catalog constraints.
prompt: Design the machine-learning system that ranks results after a search service retrieves eligible candidates.
productGoal: Help a user satisfy an expressed query with minimal reformulation.
Clarify whether the corpus is documents, products, jobs, or another entity.
Define policy, availability, and freshness constraints before model scoring.
predictionTarget: Predict graded relevance or a useful downstream action conditioned on query and result.
Consider separate targets for navigational, informational, and transactional intents.
Keep retrieval eligibility and business constraints explicit.
successMetrics: Offline: NDCG, MAP, MRR, recall, and calibrated human relevance judgments.
Online: successful sessions, conversion where appropriate, and reformulation reduction.
Guardrails: latency, zero-result rate, unsafe exposure, and seller or source concentration.
dataSources: Queries, retrieved candidates, impressions, positions, interactions, result content, and freshness state.
Human relevance judgments for unbiased evaluation and rare queries.
Point-in-time corpus snapshots for reproducible training.
labeling: Debias behavior labels for position and selection effects.
Use graded human labels with written rubrics for benchmark sets.
Treat abandonment carefully because it may indicate satisfaction or failure.
features: Lexical match, semantic similarity, quality, freshness, query intent, and context.
Cross-encoder or interaction features may improve precision at higher serving cost.
Query and document features must share tokenization and versioning.
baseline: Start with a lexical ranker such as BM25 plus deterministic policy filters.
Compare ML gains against the baseline by query frequency and intent segment.
modelDiscussion: Learning-to-rank trees offer strong tabular baselines and interpretability.
Neural encoders can improve semantic matching, often as retrieval or reranking stages.
A cascade can reserve expensive scoring for top candidates.
training: Build query-result examples from logged candidate sets, not only clicked results.
Version relevance labels, corpus, features, and retrieval configuration.
Use temporal splits when content and intent drift quickly.
evaluation: Evaluate head, torso, and tail queries separately.
Track retrieval recall so ranking is not blamed for absent candidates.
Use interleaving or controlled experiments when suitable for faster online comparison.
serving: Retrieve broadly, compute bounded features, rank, then apply final policy.
Cache query-independent document features and popular-query retrieval results with freshness limits.
Fall back to lexical ranking when model or feature services fail.
monitoring: Monitor query mix, feature missingness, score and rank movement, latency, and result diversity.
Maintain a stable human-labeled evaluation set plus fresh slices.
Alert on index-model version incompatibility.
feedbackLoop: Log every eligible shown result and its position.
Use exploration or randomized buckets to estimate less-biased preferences.
Review model changes that could amplify incumbent exposure.
failureModes: Retriever recall drops after an index rollout.
Behavior labels teach position bias.
A new content type lacks required features.
An expensive reranker exceeds tail-latency budgets.
tradeoffs: Semantic relevance can cost more latency than lexical scoring.
Fresh features improve timeliness but reduce cache reuse.
Behavior labels scale, while judged labels are cleaner but costly.
extensions: How would query autocomplete connect without leaking private queries?
How would multilingual ranking change evaluation?
How would sponsored results remain separately governed?
interviewChecklist: Designed fallback and index-model compatibility checks.

title: Fraud Detection
summary: Score risky transactions under asymmetric cost, delayed labels, and adversarial behavior.
prompt: Design an ML system that scores payment transactions for fraud and supports approve, review, or decline decisions.
productGoal: Reduce preventable fraud loss without blocking legitimate customers.
Define which transactions, regions, and payment methods are in scope.
Clarify whether the model advises a policy engine or makes the final action.
predictionTarget: Estimate fraud risk within a defined outcome window.
Model action costs: false declines, review expense, fraud loss, and customer friction.
Separate risk score from policy thresholds so operations can adapt safely.
successMetrics: Offline: precision and recall at operational thresholds, PR-AUC, and expected cost.
Online: fraud loss rate, approval rate, review yield, and customer friction.
Guardrails: latency, review queue size, segment fairness, and rule/model disagreement.
dataSources: Transaction attributes, account history, device and network signals, merchant context, and prior outcomes.
Use only signals legally and operationally available at decision time.
Protect highly sensitive fields with strict access and retention controls.
labeling: Labels may arrive from chargebacks, investigations, or customer reports with long delay.
Not all declined transactions receive observable outcomes, creating selective-label bias.
Track label maturity and train on cohorts whose outcome window has closed.
features: Velocity aggregates, account age, device relationships, amount deviation, and merchant history.
Graph features may surface coordinated behavior but require freshness and privacy design.
Point-in-time aggregation is essential to prevent leakage.
baseline: Start with reviewed deterministic rules and a simple calibrated classifier.
Compare incremental value over the rules that already route known patterns.
modelDiscussion: Gradient-boosted trees are a practical baseline for heterogeneous tabular signals.
Graph or sequence models may add signal when coordinated histories justify complexity.
Calibrated outputs make threshold and cost decisions easier to reason about.
training: Build mature, point-in-time examples with stable entity resolution.
Retrain when attack behavior or product mix changes, with champion-challenger rollout.
Keep rules, model, features, and policy versions linked for audit.
evaluation: Use temporal validation and stress emerging attack patterns.
Report threshold curves and expected cost, not a single accuracy number.
Evaluate by geography, merchant type, new users, and other meaningful segments.
serving: Fetch online velocity and entity features under a strict decision deadline.
Score, calibrate, and pass risk plus reason codes to a policy engine.
Define conservative fallback rules for missing critical features or model timeout.
monitoring: Monitor feature health, decision distribution, approval rate, review volume, and delayed fraud outcomes.
Track policy and model contribution separately.
Detect sudden entity or network shifts that may signal an attack.
feedbackLoop: Feed completed investigations and mature chargebacks back with event-time correctness.
Avoid training directly on past policy decisions without accounting for censored outcomes.
Use analyst feedback with quality review because investigator labels can drift.
failureModes: Delayed labels hide a new attack for weeks.
A feature outage causes a broad false-decline spike.
Attackers adapt to visible decision boundaries.
Review capacity collapses after a threshold change.
tradeoffs: More aggressive blocking reduces fraud but raises customer harm.
Fresh cross-entity signals improve detection while increasing latency and privacy risk.
Frequent retraining adapts faster but raises validation and stability burden.
extensions: How would manual review prioritization work?
How would you evaluate a policy change with selective labels?
How would real-time graph signals be served?
interviewChecklist: Covered adversarial drift and review capacity.

title: Spam and Abuse Detection
summary: Detect harmful content and behavior with layered models, policy context, and human review.
prompt: Design an ML system that identifies spam or abusive content before and after publication.
productGoal: Reduce harmful exposure while preserving legitimate expression.
Define content modalities, languages, and enforcement actions.
Treat policy definitions and appeals as core system inputs, not model afterthoughts.
predictionTarget: Predict policy-category risk and severity, potentially as a multilabel output.
Distinguish content classification from account-level coordinated behavior.
Use confidence and severity to route allow, reduce, review, or block actions.
successMetrics: Offline: per-policy precision, recall, F1, calibration, and language or segment slices.
Online: harmful exposure prevalence, appeal overturn rate, and review yield.
Guardrails: latency, legitimate-content removal, reviewer load, and creator impact.
dataSources: Content, metadata, account history, reports, moderation actions, and appeal outcomes.
Limit access to private content and redact unnecessary identifiers.
Separate user reports from confirmed policy violations.
labeling: Use trained reviewers with policy-specific rubrics and disagreement adjudication.
Appeals can correct labels but reflect a selected subset.
Refresh benchmark sets as policies and abuse tactics evolve.
features: Text or media representations, account velocity, link reputation, and network signals.
Language and locale context can be critical for meaning.
Avoid leaking post-enforcement signals into pre-publication training examples.
baseline: Begin with high-precision rules for known abusive signatures plus a simple text classifier.
Measure each layer's marginal value and false-positive burden.
modelDiscussion: Use cascades: inexpensive rules and models first, richer classifiers for ambiguous cases.
Account and graph models can complement content models for coordinated spam.
Calibrate per policy or language when score meaning differs.
training: Version policy taxonomy with training labels.
Sample both naturally occurring content and difficult reviewed cases.
Retrain through controlled releases with reviewer and appeal feedback.
evaluation: Report per-policy and per-language results, including low-prevalence precision.
Stress adversarial obfuscation and distribution shift.
Human review remains necessary for nuanced policies and model audits.
serving: Run low-latency pre-publication checks and deeper asynchronous post-publication review.
Route uncertain high-severity cases to human review.
Provide safe fallback behavior if language detection or model serving fails.
monitoring: Monitor policy prevalence, score distributions, enforcement rate, appeals, and reviewer queues.
Detect sudden changes by language, client, or content source.
Audit sampled allowed and removed content for blind spots.
feedbackLoop: Incorporate adjudicated reviews and appeals after quality controls.
Avoid allowing mass reports to become unverified truth.
Use active learning to select informative uncertain examples without overfitting reviewer queues.
failureModes: A coordinated campaign shifts wording faster than retraining.
A language detector routes content to the wrong model.
Reports are weaponized against legitimate users.
A threshold update overwhelms human review.
tradeoffs: Pre-publication enforcement reduces exposure but has stricter latency and false-positive costs.
One global model is simpler; policy and language specialization may perform more reliably.
Automation scales while human review handles nuance and appeals.
extensions: How would image or video moderation join the cascade?
How would appeals update labels safely?
How would you detect coordinated accounts?
interviewChecklist: Included appeals, abuse of reports, and reviewer capacity.

title: Feed Ranking
summary: Rank a dynamic candidate set while balancing relevance, freshness, diversity, and ecosystem health.
prompt: Design the ML ranking system for a personalized feed assembled from followed and recommended sources.
productGoal: Help users find timely, valuable content in a finite session.
Define whether candidates come from a follow graph, recommendations, or both.
Include diversity, integrity, and source exposure constraints.
predictionTarget: Estimate multiple outcomes such as meaningful engagement, hide risk, and session value.
Avoid using dwell time as an unquestioned proxy for satisfaction.
Keep candidate eligibility and ranking objectives separately governed.
successMetrics: Offline: ranking quality, calibration, candidate recall, and diversity measures.
Online: qualified engagement, return behavior, and explicit satisfaction signals.
Guardrails: hides, reports, latency, freshness, and source concentration.
dataSources: Feed impressions, positions, interactions, content metadata, graph relationships, and session context.
Log candidates considered, not only winners.
Use point-in-time features for rapidly changing content and graph state.
labeling: Build multitask labels with explicit observation windows.
Correct position and repeated-exposure bias.
Treat missing interaction differently from explicit negative feedback.
features: User-author affinity, content embeddings, freshness, social context, and session behavior.
Real-time session features can adapt quickly but raise serving complexity.
Policy and availability features should gate or constrain scoring.
baseline: Start with reverse-chronological followed content plus simple freshness and quality rules.
Use the baseline to expose the real value and cost of personalization.
modelDiscussion: A candidate mixer can combine graph, retrieval, and exploration sources.
A multitask ranker can predict several outcomes before a constrained value function.
A final policy layer enforces diversity and integrity rules.
training: Create point-in-time examples from logged candidate sets.
Train on rolling windows to follow changing content while retaining stability.
Version objective weights and policy with the model.
evaluation: Evaluate source recall, ranker quality, and final policy output separately.
Slice by new users, creator size, session depth, and content freshness.
Use long-enough experiments to observe more than immediate clicks.
serving: Fetch several candidate sources in parallel with strict time budgets.
Hydrate online features, rank a bounded set, then apply constraints.
Fall back to chronological followed content if personalized stages fail.
monitoring: Monitor source timeouts, candidate mix, feature freshness, score distribution, and final exposure.
Track delayed satisfaction and integrity outcomes by model version.
Alert on concentration or fallback changes even if CTR is stable.
feedbackLoop: Repeated exposure can create popularity loops, so log and limit recurrence.
Exploration can gather information for new content within safety boundaries.
Negative feedback should update both ranking and candidate-source policy.
failureModes: One candidate source times out and silently disappears.
A short-term objective promotes sensational content.
Fresh posts lack embeddings or quality features.
Objective-weight changes shift ecosystem exposure unexpectedly.
tradeoffs: Real-time features improve session adaptation but cost latency and operational complexity.
Multi-objective scoring is flexible but harder to calibrate and explain.
Diversity constraints can reduce immediate predicted engagement while improving discovery.
extensions: How would exploration be introduced?
How would you evaluate creator ecosystem health?
How would integrity classifiers interact with ranking?

title: Semantic Search
summary: Retrieve meaningfully related documents using embeddings while preserving freshness and lexical precision.
prompt: Design a semantic search system for a large document corpus using embedding-based retrieval.
productGoal: Return relevant documents even when query and document wording differ.
Clarify corpus size, update rate, languages, and access controls.
Define whether semantic retrieval augments or replaces lexical search.
predictionTarget: Estimate query-document relevance for candidate retrieval and optional reranking.
Optimize candidate recall before applying expensive precision stages.
Respect document eligibility and permission filters at every stage.
successMetrics: Offline: recall at K, NDCG, MAP, and human relevance judgments.
Online: successful search sessions, result engagement, and reformulation reduction.
Guardrails: latency, index freshness, permission leakage, and zero-result behavior.
dataSources: Document text and metadata, queries, impressions, interactions, and judged query-document pairs.
Corpus snapshots and embedding versions must be reproducible.
Private corpora require tenant and document access boundaries.
labeling: Use human relevance judgments for a stable benchmark.
Behavior data needs exposure and position correction.
Mine hard negatives from confusing retrieved candidates rather than only random documents.
features: Dense query and document embeddings, lexical scores, metadata, freshness, and quality.
Chunk-level representations may help long documents but require document-level aggregation.
Language and domain adaptation can matter more than model size.
baseline: Use a lexical search engine as the primary baseline.
Compare dense-only and hybrid retrieval before adding a reranker.
modelDiscussion: A bi-encoder supports fast approximate nearest-neighbor retrieval.
A cross-encoder can rerank a small candidate set at greater cost.
Hybrid fusion preserves exact terms while adding semantic recall.
training: Train or adapt encoders from judged pairs and carefully sampled hard negatives.
Version model, tokenizer, chunking, and corpus snapshot together.
Re-embed the corpus through staged index migration when representations change.
evaluation: Measure retrieval recall before reranker metrics.
Slice by query length, language, freshness, and rare terminology.
Evaluate permission filters independently from relevance.
serving: Encode the query, retrieve from a versioned ANN index, fuse lexical candidates, and rerank if budget permits.
Cache popular query embeddings with versioned keys.
Fall back to lexical results during embedding or ANN failure.
monitoring: Monitor embedding latency, index freshness, candidate counts, score drift, and lexical fallback.
Run a fixed judged set against every index and model version.
Audit access-filter correctness continuously.
feedbackLoop: Collect impressions and interactions with retrieval-stage provenance.
Use failed queries and reformulations to expand evaluation coverage.
Avoid learning private query-document associations across tenants.
failureModes: New documents wait too long for embedding and indexing.
A model update is incompatible with the existing vector index.
ANN tuning lowers recall to meet latency.
Post-retrieval permission filtering leaves too few results.
tradeoffs: Dense retrieval improves semantic matching while lexical search preserves exact rare terms.
Frequent index updates improve freshness but fragment or complicate serving.
A reranker improves precision but increases tail latency.
extensions: How would multilingual embeddings change the index?
How would you support document deletion guarantees?
When should chunk results be collapsed to documents?
interviewChecklist: Protected access boundaries and fallback behavior.

title: RAG Knowledge Assistant
summary: Build a permission-aware assistant that retrieves evidence and generates grounded answers over an evolving corpus.
prompt: Design a retrieval-augmented knowledge assistant that answers questions from an organization's documents and cites its evidence.
productGoal: Help users find grounded answers from content they are allowed to access.
Clarify corpus types, freshness, answer latency, and when the system should abstain.
Treat citations, permissions, and auditability as product requirements.
predictionTarget: Retrieval should identify evidence-bearing chunks; generation should produce an answer supported by that evidence.
Reranking can estimate question-chunk relevance before context construction.
The system needs an abstention or clarification decision when evidence is insufficient.
successMetrics: Retrieval: evidence recall and ranking quality on representative questions.
Generation: groundedness, citation correctness, answer usefulness, and abstention quality.
System guardrails: latency, cost, permission violations, unsafe output, and fallback rate.
dataSources: Permissioned documents, metadata, access-control state, user questions, retrieved chunks, citations, and reviewed outcomes.
Ingestion must retain document version and source identity.
Logs should minimize sensitive text and follow retention policy.
labeling: Build evaluation questions with expected evidence and acceptable answer criteria.
Use expert or trained review for groundedness and citation judgments.
Separate retrieval failure from generation failure in labels.
features: Chunk embeddings, lexical scores, document metadata, recency, authority, and query intent.
Rerank with query-chunk interactions when latency allows.
Access attributes must be enforced as filters, not optional ranking features.
baseline: Start with permission-filtered lexical retrieval and an extractive evidence view.
Add generation only after retrieval quality and citation behavior are measurable.
modelDiscussion: Chunking strategy should follow document structure and answer granularity rather than one universal size.
Hybrid retrieval can combine exact terminology with semantic recall.
Context construction should deduplicate, preserve source boundaries, and fit a controlled token budget.
training: Most first versions can use existing embedding, reranking, and generation models with evaluated prompts.
If adapting models, version datasets, prompts, chunking, and model artifacts together.
Re-index documents when embedding or chunking versions change.
evaluation: Run retrieval-only, generation-with-gold-evidence, and end-to-end evaluations.
Include unanswerable, conflicting, stale, permissioned, and multi-document questions.
Use human review for nuanced usefulness while keeping reproducible automated checks.
serving: Authenticate, resolve access scope, retrieve, rerank, construct context, generate, and attach citations.
Cache document parsing and embeddings; cache answers only with permission, version, and freshness-aware keys.
Stream generation only after permission-filtered context is fixed and logged safely.
monitoring: Monitor ingestion lag, embedding/index versions, retrieval scores, citation coverage, latency by stage, token use, and abstention.
Sample answers for groundedness and permission audit.
Trace stages with document IDs and versions while avoiding unnecessary content capture.
feedbackLoop: Collect structured helpfulness and citation feedback, not unrestricted private notes.
Route reported answers to reviewed evaluation sets before retraining or prompt changes.
Use low-confidence and failed-retrieval cases to improve corpus and test coverage.
failureModes: A document permission changes but stale index filters still expose it.
Poor chunk boundaries split the evidence needed for an answer.
Retrieval finds related but non-evidentiary text and generation hallucinates a bridge.
A popular question causes expensive repeated generation.
Observability logs capture sensitive document text.
tradeoffs: Larger chunks provide context but reduce retrieval precision and consume more tokens.
Reranking improves evidence quality while adding latency and cost.
Answer caching saves cost but is risky across permissions and rapidly changing documents.
Aggressive generation is more responsive; abstention is safer when evidence is weak.
extensions: How would document-level access revocation propagate?
How would conversational follow-ups retain safe context?
How would conflicting sources be surfaced?
How would tool use be isolated from document retrieval?
interviewChecklist: Defined ingestion, chunking, and document versions.
Separated retrieval, reranking, context, and generation.
Evaluated retrieval and grounded generation independently.
Covered hallucination, latency, caching, observability, and abstention.
